title: I spent 2 years developing this game using AI.
author: Equivalent-Visual510

comments.author: Kitchen-Many-8466
comments.body: what was the moment it stopped being a shortcut and started being a tax? like where did you spend more time fighting the tool than it saved you

replies.author: Equivalent-Visual510
replies.body:
For me, the biggest 'tax' was during the first year. AI tools were still pretty early in their development, and I was using Cursor at the time. It often turned into a nightmare where asking the AI to fix one bug would somehow spawn 50 new ones. I struggled with it so much, and ran into core issues the AI just couldn't resolve, that I actually had to step away and abandon the project for a few months.

Later on, I came back with newer tools like Antigravity and eventually Codex, which finally helped me untangle that mess and fix the lingering issues. But the consequences were real—the game initially got hit with low ratings on Google Play because of the bugs that had slipped through during that messy phase.

replies.author: Kitchen-Many-8466
replies.body:
That matches what I've seen from other people who were on the early Cursor train. The tool had no real model of your architecture, so it would "fix" a function in isolation and not understand that three other systems depended on its side effects. In a combat AI system with state machines and cooldown timers, that's especially brutal because the bugs are timing-related and don't show up in a single test run.

The months away probably did you a favor. When you came back and the tools had gotten better at maintaining context across files, you could actually use them for the parts they're good at (boilerplate, straightforward logic) without them silently corrupting your state management.

replies.author: Equivalent-Visual510
replies.body: Spot on. The silent corruption of the state management was exactly what drove me crazy back then. Waiting for the tools to improve their multi-file context windows was probably the best decision I accidentally made!

replies.author: Equivalent-Visual510
replies.body:
About a year ago when AI wasn't as capable, I mainly used Antigravity and Cursor, just knocking out tasks one by one.

Nowadays, I rely entirely on GPT-6 Sol. My workflow is to first discuss my overall intentions with it, have it create a solid plan, and then jump straight into coding. I actually used to have a setup very similar to yours—using Sol to delegate tasks to sub-agents like Luna—but I found it a bit too cumbersome and it burned through tokens way too fast. Now, I just stick to one single AI for both planning and implementation. It keeps things much more streamlined.

Regarding the art strategy: as you probably know, AI still struggles a lot with generating good pixel art. Because of that, I usually buy pre-made asset packs to use as a baseline, and then I manually draw and edit over those templates to fit exactly what I need.

Since you're already using Sol for architecture, switching to it as your main chat might simplify your pipeline and save some tokens. Hope this helps!

comments.author: Tom_Baron
comments.body:
I like your commitment to gameplay development!

In my professional role I am an analyst and build processes using AI currently. When im building out a process, i pass claude our company branding doc. Let it use that to make the css for the dashboard then allllll my time is spent designing and optimising the process.

So when i started building games for fun, visuals and sound came second. 

Ive spent probably 100 hours so far watching 30vs30 npcs playing my game in a sim mode I designed. Tuning gameplay, looking for holes in npc behavior, getting one side to employ certain strategies and A/B testing them, rolling those strategies into their modelling. 

Im mid way through putting a whole layer on top of the core tactical gameplay now and will likely spend far more time than I have watching matches play out 😆 .

But yes, the most beautiful artwork in the world is wasted if your game plays terribly or the core idea is dull and boring.

replies.author: Equivalent-Visual510
replies.body:
Thank you so much! Honestly, this means a lot after grinding solo for months.

To be completely honest, a huge inspiration for the combat came from Elden Ring! I really wanted to see what happens when you bring Souls-like combat mechanics into an autonomous tactical auto-battler:

1. Souls-inspired combat: Every soldier has an actual stamina bar. They do not just trade blows mindlessly - they perform tactical dodge rolls with invincibility frames (I-frames), raise shields to block incoming damage, and manage their stamina. If their stamina runs dry, they are forced to rely heavily on desperate blocking while recovering.

2. Dynamic battlefield momentum: The units actively read the state of the fight. When our squad has the advantage, soldiers turn hyper-aggressive, relentlessly pressing forward to finish off the enemy. But when our squad is losing or outnumbered, frontline units automatically switch to a defensive stance - blocking much more frequently to buy time and tank damage so our backline archers can shoot safely from behind.

3. Subtle footsies: Instead of standing frozen while waiting on attack cooldowns, units orbit around their opponent to adjust angles, making clashes look like active fencing.

Blending Elden Ring combat depth with autonomous squad AI was a massive headache to balance, but seeing comments like yours makes every late night worth it! Hope you enjoy the game!
